name: Clean runs of the rota
brief:
A support team's rota lists who is on call each day. Management wants to know how many runs of consecutive days, of any length, have nobody on call twice. Runs that cover different days count separately, even when the names match.

Write `count_clean_runs(rota)`, which returns that count, or 0 for an empty rota.

Example. For `rota = ['ana', 'ben', 'ana']` the runs `ana`, `ben`, `ana`, `ana, ben` and `ben, ana` are clean. The whole rota repeats ana, so the answer is 5.
constraints: $0 \le n \le 200{,}000$ days, names strings or whole numbers. Answers can pass $10^{10}$.
$O(n)$ time is the target. Checking every run is too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Keep a dict from each name to the last day it appeared, and a left edge that jumps past a repeat. Each new day ends as many clean runs as there are days from the left edge to today.

examples.note: Three single days and the two pairs are clean; the run of all three repeats ana.
Only the two single days are clean, because the pair repeats ana.

how: Submit runs 13 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: Every clean run ends on some day, and the clean runs ending there start anywhere from the left edge to that day.
Each day adds `day - left + 1` runs, not 1, and the left edge only moves forward: check `last[name] >= left`.
Each day is one dict look-up and one addition, so the work is $O(n)$.

planted.slip: It extends a run from every start day until a name repeats, which is right but quadratic when the names rarely repeat.
